narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 72.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the review process treated your profile as carrying a high risk of bar-exam failure, and the admissions decision followed that risk assessment.

The strongest factor driving that prediction was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. That standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the next most influential factor. At 25.5, it is well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so it also pushed the assessment toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was slightly below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but among the top three factors it was the only one that pushed toward passing; its positive effect was simply not enough to outweigh the other two signals.

To improve a future application, focus on strengthening the areas the review weighted most heavily: raise your LSAT score if possible, and address your academic standing in later coursework through a post-baccalaureate or master’s program that demonstrates sustained improvement. You should also consider applying to schools with more flexible admission criteria and seeking advising about bar-exam preparation and application narratives that explain your trajectory.
